By default, when a sandbox idles without a command, Render automatically snapshots and suspends it, and then wakes it back up on the next command. Importantly, you don’t pay for CPU or memory while a sandbox is suspended. (The default idle timeout of 15 minutes is configurable, and auto-suspend is optional.)

## Keep each sandbox secure

Agents often need network access and API keys to do useful work. Render Sandboxes let you grant them both, while controlling where each sandbox can send data and the keys it can see. # Introducing Render Sandboxes: A computer for every agent

November 04, 2026

· Yaroslav Borets, Ammar Aijazi, and Azzam Aijazi

Today we’re launching Render Sandboxes in public beta. Render Sandboxes let you safely give your agents a computer to work with: a fully isolated Linux environment where they can install dependencies, edit files, and run code.

Each sandbox starts quickly, runs indefinitely, and automatically suspends when idle. You can reliably run thousands at once and lock down what each one can reach. You’re billed for CPU only when your agents are actually using it. [...] Render Sandboxes work with any agent harness and model. You can operate sandboxes through the TypeScript or Python SDK, or the Render CLI.

Check out our quickstart, or share this prompt with your coding agent:

## Agents need a computer of their own

Agents doing complex work need a separate machine for each task or user, isolated from your app and from each other. And since agent work comes in bursts, those machines need to start and stop with demand.

A web service isn’t built for this. Its instances stay up and serve all your users, and a new deploy can take minutes.

Render Sandboxes give each user or task its own machine the moment it’s needed. Each sandbox runs in its own Firecracker microVM.

Product brief

## What Render Sandboxesdoes.

Render Sandboxes give every agent its own isolated Linux computer. Sandboxes starts in under a second and can run any agent or harness, like Claude Code or Codex. Your agent can also run your app with Docker Compose to test its changes. You decide which domains each sandbox can reach. When your agent goes idle, the sandbox suspends and compute charges stop. It wakes with files and memory intact. And you can reliably run thousands at once - all on the same platform as the rest of your app.

Which agents can run in Render Sandboxes?

Render Sandboxes is described as supporting any agent or harness, with Claude Code and Codex given as examples.

The product description states that sandboxes start in under a second.

What happens when an agent becomes idle?

Its sandbox suspends and compute charges stop. When it wakes, its files and memory remain intact.

Yes. Agents can run your application with Docker Compose inside the sandbox to test their changes.

results.title: How to Run Untrusted Code Safely in Production with AI Sandboxes | Modal Blog
results.content: Active-resource pricing: Untrusted code is unpredictable: one execution prints a result in milliseconds, the next installs packages or loops until it hits a limit, and agents often sit idle between runs waiting on model responses. Fixed-reservation pricing, the model most Sandbox providers use, pushes teams to reserve for the heaviest run, so utilization stays low and costs run high relative to the work done. Modal's active-resourcing model lets sandboxes start from a configured CPU and memory baseline and burst above it automatically, so teams provision for typical usage instead of peak usage and face less risk of out-of-memory failures. Billing is per second on the greater of requested and actual resources. [...] Modal bills sandboxes on active resources: each one has a requested CPU and memory baseline, can burst past it automatically when a piece of untrusted code turns out to be heavier than expected, and is charged per second for whichever is greater, the requested or the actual resources. That bursting also makes out-of-memory failures less likely when generated code spikes. Teams can therefore size sandboxes around typical executions and still cover peak executions. Most Sandbox providers charge for a fixed reservation that code cannot exceed, so teams running untrusted code have to reserve for the largest execution they expect and pay for capacity that sits unused on every smaller run.
